messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had been at the factory for nearly six years, working the late shift on a line that kept her on her feet under fluorescent lights and the constant churn of machinery. Before the trauma, she had lived with her younger brother Luis in a small apartment and had been the kind of woman coworkers described as cheerful, quick to laugh, the one who brought food to share on birthdays. That changed the night Luis died unexpectedly after a collapse at home. One moment he was complaining of chest discomfort over the phone, sounding annoyed more than frightened, and the next Marisol was on the line with emergency services, hearing sirens grow louder outside her building while she stood helpless in the hallway, staring at the door as if it might open and undo what was happening. By the time the paramedics left, Luis was gone. Afterward, funerals, cemeteries, and even the smallest grief-related conversation seemed to carry her back to that night with terrible force; if a coworker mentioned losing a parent, if a church announcement referred to a memorial, if she passed a graveyard on the way to work, her body tightened and she felt herself pulled back into the moment when sirens had filled the street and her brother had not come back.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol began going over and over the details of the event, replaying every minute as if a hidden clue might explain why he died and whether she had missed something. She asked the dispatcher why the ambulance had taken so long, asked her sister whether Luis had seemed “off” earlier, and asked friends to reassure her that she was okay, that she had not somehow caused the death by waiting too long to push harder for help. Anything that reminded her of someone she had lost became something she avoided without much thought: she stopped attending family gatherings where people spoke openly about the dead, declined invitations to church memorials, and changed the route she took home so she would not pass the cemetery near her neighborhood. These efforts brought only brief relief. The more she searched for certainty, the more she found herself dwelling on the same unanswered questions, and the more she heard other people talk about loss, the more convinced she became that the world had already decided she would keep losing people. She had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere, that the happy version of herself had ended with Luis, and that her life had been destroyed by the trauma in a way that could not be repaired.

Those beliefs made the triggers sharper still. When an ambulance passed the factory during her shift, the siren would cut through the noise of the machines and she would freeze, feeling as though everyone around her had moved into a life from which she had been excluded. At funerals or even in a passing conversation about bereavement, she felt herself bracing for another collapse, another absence, another reason to think she was meant to stand outside of ordinary life. Because she believed she no longer belonged anywhere and that everything had been ruined, the sirens, graves, and loss talk no longer felt like isolated reminders; they seemed like evidence that the rest of the world was still in motion while hers had stopped. Then she would spend hours afterward turning the event over again, trying to make sense of the details and asking anyone nearby if she seemed all right, if she looked unsteady, if they thought she was “normal.” Those questions soothed her only for a moment. They also deepened the sense that something in her had changed permanently, reinforcing her conviction that she used to be a happy person and now was always miserable.

By the time she came to treatment, Marisol had become increasingly withdrawn at work, missing breaks to sit alone in the restroom whenever talk of illness or funerals drifted through the lunchroom. She was exhausted by the effort of avoiding reminders, exhausted by the constant checking of her own reactions, and frightened that one more siren, one more grave, one more conversation about loss would confirm what she already feared: that her life had been irreversibly destroyed and that she would keep living as someone who no longer had a place. What brought her in was the realization that she could not keep asking everyone around her for reassurance and still feel any closer to being okay. What she most hoped for was to believe, even a little, that Luis’s death had not erased her future.
